subject: Record visibility & erasure paths for customer queries
messages:
From: Erin Patel <erin.patel@brightbank.com>
To: laura_bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
Cc: BrightBank Security <security@brightbank.com>
Date: Mon, 14 Dec 2026 09:12:00 -05:00
Subject: Clarify exactly what Redwood keeps by default (requests / outputs / streaming)

Hi Laura,

We're working through our GDPR mapping and have a couple of targeted questions about Redwood's default retention behavior for hosted deployments. Can you confirm, with examples, what is retained by default and where, specifically:

- User requests / prompts vs. final model outputs (are both kept?)
- Intermediate streaming tokens or partial responses (are those persisted?)
- KV cache / session artifacts tied to a conversation (persisted between sessions?)
- Attachments uploaded to a request (are these stored?)

Also: if a customer triggers an account-level erasure request, what is the deletion/verification workflow and typical time-to-purge for hosted accounts? Please include examples (e.g., a user requests full erasure; how long until logs/outputs are gone and what audit evidence do you provide).

We need a concise summary we can include in our vendor profile and one example flow that we can pass to our legal team. If you have a short one-page summary or diagram, that would help.

Thanks — Erin
Erin Patel
Head of Cloud Security, BrightBank
From: laura_bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
To: Erin Patel <erin.patel@brightbank.com>
Cc: BrightBank Security <security@brightbank.com>
Date: Mon, 14 Dec 2026 11:07:00 -05:00
Subject: Re: Clarify exactly what Redwood keeps by default (requests / outputs / streaming)

Hi Erin — thanks for the clear list. Putting a short, concrete summary below and attaching a one-pager (Redwood_Retention_Summary.pdf). If you'd like, we can also run a 30-minute call with product/security to walk the flow for your legal/compliance teams.

High-level (hosted API, default settings):
- Request inputs (user prompts) and final model outputs: retained by default for 90 days. These are stored in our telemetry store for debugging, billing, and quality monitoring.
- Streaming tokens / partial responses: transient; kept for up to 24 hours strictly for request replay and real-time debugging, then purged. Not used for indexing.
- KV cache / session artifacts: ephemeral. Not persisted to long-term storage after session termination unless the customer explicitly enables session snapshots for debugging or session replay.
- Attachments uploaded in a request: stored encrypted at rest; retained for 90 days by default. We surface names and hashes in the UI and purge the blobs on erasure.

Erasure workflow (hosted):
1) Customer submits erasure via console or support ticket and completes identity verification.
2) We schedule a verified purge job; primary telemetry and blob stores are queued for deletion.
3) Purge completes and tombstones are applied; engineering review occurs if any manual artifacts were exported.
4) Customer receives confirmation email and an audit token (job id) that can be used to reference the deletion.

Typical SLA: ~30 calendar days from verification to completed purge + audit token. We can provide a signed attestation for enterprise contracts on request.

I'll loop in our product/security folks for any technical clarifications.

Best,
Laura
Laura Bennett
Director, Product Partnerships
Redwood Inference

Subject: Fwd: Clarify exactly what Redwood keeps by default (requests / outputs / streaming)

Team — forwarding Erin's questions (below). Drafted a concise customer-facing summary in my reply (attached). A couple of asks before I send the formal note / one-pager to BrightBank's legal team:

1) Is the 90-day default for requests + outputs accurate and OK to ship as the default statement for hosted customers? I intentionally used 90 days (vs. 45) because we rely on that window for billing reconciliation + quality regression detection on production.

2) For streaming tokens and partial responses: calling them "transient (up to 24h)" — is that precise from an implementation standpoint? I want to avoid saying we persist partial tokens beyond debugging windows.

3) Erasure workflow: I wrote ~30 days post-verification. Please confirm realistic upper bound and whether we should say "up to 30 calendar days" or a softer "~30 calendar days". Also flag any manual steps that require SOC2 controls to be mentioned.

Quoted for context: 
> On Mon, Dec 14, 2026 at 09:12 -05:00 Erin Patel <erin.patel@brightbank.com> wrote:
> > We're working through our GDPR mapping ... (see original for full list)

TIA — LMK if you prefer different language and I'll incorporate.

— Laura
From: kimberly_park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
To: laura_bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, marissa_cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 14 Dec 2026 12:45:00 -05:00
Subject: Re: Fwd: Clarify exactly what Redwood keeps by default (requests / outputs / streaming)

Laura / team — quick confirmations from security/product perspective:

- 90 days for request inputs + final outputs (hosted, default): acceptable to present as the default retention for hosted customers. We should add a single line noting customers can request shorter windows via a retention setting on the account.
- Streaming tokens / partial responses: implementation keeps these in-memory and in a short-lived trace store for up to 24 hours solely for replay/debugging. We do not index or persist them to long-term telemetry.
- KV cache / session artifacts: ephemeral by default. Clarify that Dedicated customers can opt into session snapshot persistence for debugging, which stores snapshots to a customer-scoped blob with retention either customer-controlled or defaulting to 90 days.
- Attachments: yes, stored encrypted. Note that attachments are processed (hashing/metadata extraction) and we retain both blobs and derived metadata; both are purged on erasure.

Erasure timing: security confirms the operational pathway is typically complete within 30 calendar days after verification. For complex cases (exports, data held for legal reasons, or multi-tenant backups) we should say 'up to 60 days' as the upper bound. Recommend language: "Standard verified erasure completes within 30 calendar days; complex scenarios may take up to 60 days."

I'll review the one-pager and add SOC2 references where appropriate.

— Kim
